per_ply.system_comment: White missed the potential to strip Black of the bishop-pair edge—a coordination edge that often matters in the middlegame—and to reach a bishop-for-knight structure that could have led toward equality. Instead 10.f4 concedes a clear advantage to Black ((+0.06 → -0.81, Stockfish:16), [pv:f4 d5 Bb3 f6 fxe5]): the f-file opens for the rook, but White's pieces are now more passive, and the pawn push may eventually yield a passed pawn on e5. 10.Bb3 leads to equality ([pv:Bb3 a5 a3 Bxc3 bxc3]).

The most accurate move is 11.bxc3, which may lead to more active rooks on the open files as the line unfolds — activity on open files often pays off once lines clear — though it still leads to a slight advantage for Black (-0.40, Stockfish:16) along [pv:bxc3 d5 Bb3 a5 exd5]. Bxf7+ was clearly weaker, leading to a clear advantage for Black along [pv:Bxf7+ Rxf7 bxc3 exf4 Qd2].

per_ply.system_comment: White's most accurate move is fxe5, which leads to a slight advantage for Black (-0.45, Stockfish:16) along [pv:fxe5 fxg5 Rxf8+ Kxf8 Qf3+]. White immediately targets the rook on f8, and the line may leave Black's back rank vulnerable—a lasting worry when the king lacks escape squares—in return for Black having won a piece for a pawn and White leaving a piece hanging. Qh5 is a comparable option that leads to a clear advantage for Black along [pv:Qh5 fxg5 fxe5 Rxf1+ Rxf1], putting immediate pressure on Black's king while Black also has a hanging piece.

The most accurate move, 13...fxg5, maintains Black's advantage (-0.41, Stockfish:16) along [pv:fxg5 Rxf8+ Kxf8 Qf3+ Kg8] by making Black's rooks active on the open files—rooks on open files often control the center and support the rest of the army. Even after White's best try 14.Rxf8+, Black can keep the edge deeper in that line. By contrast, 13...a5 would improve Black's piece activity and open the a-file for the rook, yet it leads to a clear advantage for White [pv:a5 exf6 Nxf6 a4 Be6], which is why capturing on g5 is the stronger choice.

Rxf8+ is White's most accurate try, yet it still leads to a slight advantage for Black (-0.48, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Rxf8+ Kxf8 Qf3+ Kg8 Rf1], at the cost of allowing Black to win a knight for a pawn while White's pieces become passive. Qh5 is a roughly comparable option that leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Qh5 Rxf1+ Rxf1 Be6 Qxg5], immediately putting Black's king under pressure while leaving a piece hanging.

14...Kxf8 maintains Black's advantage by making the king safe, shedding the danger that had been gathering around the monarch. With the king secure, Black can attend to the rest of the position without urgent defensive chores. (-0.44, Stockfish:16) [pv:Kxf8 Qf3+ Kg8 Rf1 Kh8] White may follow with Qf3+ in the line, though...Kg8 keeps Black holding the edge.

The most accurate move is 15.Qf3+, which immediately puts Black's king under pressure and may activate White's rooks on the open files deeper in the line, though it leads to a slight advantage for Black (-0.42, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Qf3+ Kg8 Rf1 Kh8]. King pressure often forces the defender to tie down pieces—a comparable option was 15.Qh5, which would leave Black a hanging piece and target the knight on e8, yet leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Qh5 Kg8 Qxg5 Be6 Rf1].

Black's most accurate move is 15...Kg8, which holds the balance (-0.12, Stockfish:16) and leads into [pv:Kg8 Rf1 Kh8], keeping the middlegame level as the king steps back out of the firing line. That beats 15...Nf6, which leads to a clear advantage for White after [pv:Nf6 exf6 Ng8 fxg7+ Kxg7]. From here the fight may later turn on forcing checks along the kingside.

Qf8+ leads to equality [pv:Qf8+ Qxf8 Rxf8+ Ng8 Nf3].

Nf3 was clearly weaker, leading to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Nf3 Be6 Qh5 g4 Ng5], whereas the queen check keeps the position balanced.

Rxf8+ holds the balance (-0.08, Stockfish:16), immediately putting Black's king under pressure and pinning a piece—king pressure often restricts how freely the defender's pieces can move. Nf3 was clearly weaker, leaving Black with a decisive advantage [pv:Nf3 Qf4 a4 g4 Nd4], which is why the exchange on f8 was the sounder practical choice. The queens are off — the game enters its final phase, where technique matters more than tactics. The position stays balanced.

The most accurate move, Ng8, holds the balance (-0.12, Stockfish:16) and is set to target White's rook on f8 deeper in the line [pv:Ng8 Nf3 g4 Nd4 Bd7]. Retreating the knight keeps Black's position level while setting up that idea—pressure on a rook often restricts how freely the opponent's pieces can move—a practical way to maintain equality rather than invite unnecessary risk.

Black missed the chance to pressure the knight on f3 and the potential for a safer king deeper in the line with g4. With 21...Be6, White does leave a piece hanging, but the move concedes a slight advantage to White, (-0.12 → +0.47, Stockfish:16), along [pv:Be6 Rxa8 Nxa8 Nxg5 Nc7]. g4 leads to equality along [pv:g4 Nd4 Bd7 Rxa8 Nxa8].

By contrast, the weaker Rxg8+ would leave Black with a decisive advantage [pv:Rxg8+ Bxg8 Nxg5 h6 Nf3].

The best move, 22...Nxa8, wins a knight for a pawn—a meaningful gain in an endgame—and may leave Black with an improved pawn structure deeper in the line, though at the cost of White possibly obtaining a passed pawn on d3; the result is still only a slight advantage for White (+0.49, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Nxa8 Nxg5 Nc7 Nxe6 Nxe6], with Nc7 the precise follow-up to limit the damage. By contrast, 22...g4 leaves White with a decisive advantage, merely targeting the knight on f3 after [pv:g4 Rxa7 Bc8 Ng5 Nh6], which shows why the capture was clearly stronger.

Nc7 is Black's most accurate move in this endgame, the best way to limit White to a slight advantage (+0.49, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Nc7 Nxe6 Nxe6 Bxd5 Nd8]; after Nxe6 in that line, White may gain a concrete endgame target against loose Black material. Ne7 is clearly weaker, as it gives White a winning advantage in [pv:Ne7 Nxe6 b5 Nd4 Nc7].

The most accurate move, Nxe6, maintains White's advantage (+0.52, Stockfish:16) by leaving Black with a hanging piece — a concrete endgame target White can press — along [pv:Nxe6 Nxe6 Bxd5 Nd8 Kf2], where Black's strongest reply still keeps White on top. In return, Black's king is now safer. By contrast, c4 leads to a slight advantage for Black; after [pv:c4 dxc4 Nxe6 Nxe6 Bxc4] White would eliminate the doubled pawns, though Black's pieces may become more passive deeper in that line.

24...Nxe6 is Black's strongest continuation in this endgame, though it still leads to a slight advantage for White (+0.49, Stockfish:16). After [pv:Nxe6 Bxd5 Nd8 Kf2 Ne7], Black stays in the fight while White prepares to activate his king, a typical endgame plan that slowly increases pressure; by contrast, 24...Nb5 would have been clearly weaker, giving White a winning advantage [pv:Nb5 Bxd5 Nxc3 Bxb7 Ne7].

Bxd5 is the most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage (+0.49, Stockfish:16). The line [pv:Bxd5 Nd8 Kf2 g6 Ke3] is set to activate White's king and may lead to it escorting the passed pawn forward—king activity is often decisive in such endgames. By contrast, g4 leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:g4 Ne7 a4 g6 Kf2].
